name: Dan Kegel
why_notable: American software engineer who in 1999 published 'The C10K problem', a survey of why one-thread-or-process-per-connection servers break down at around ten thousand simultaneous clients and of the operating-system interfaces (select, poll, epoll, kqueue, /dev/poll, asynchronous I/O) that fix it. The page became the standard reference for event-driven server design and helped push Linux to add epoll; servers such as nginx, and later async runtimes in Node.js, Go and Rust, follow its conclusions. It is the clearest explanation of why network I/O scales with concurrency rather than with more cores. He also created crosstool for building GCC cross-compilers and worked on Wine.
